metadata.summary: This update summarizes guidance on the diagnosis, risk assessment, treatment and follow-up of vesicoureteral reflux in children. It addresses selective imaging, bladder and bowel dysfunction, antibiotic prophylaxis and surgical options, with management adapted to clinical risk. The authors note that the evidence for many management decisions is generally of low quality.

target_population: toilet-trained children with bladder and bowel dysfunction
siblings and offspring of children with VUR

toxicities.event: Increased occurrence of non-Escherichia coli organisms

prevention: Avoid TMP-SMZ in infants aged <6 wk.
Avoid TMP-SMZ in children with severe renal insufficiency.
Prefer not to use nitrofurantoin before the age of 4 mo.
PTFE is not approved for use in children because of concern about particle migration.

toxicities.incidence: Early or delayed obstruction after Deflux injection was reported in <1% of patients; longer-term studies reported higher VUJO rates with PPC, without specifying a percentage.
recognition: Obstruction may arise late after endoscopic correction; patients with high-grade reflux and dilated ureters are at risk, and obstruction appears more common in patients with BBD.

management.actions: Temporary double-J stenting was followed by resolution.

management.severity: Cases not resolved with temporary stenting
management.actions: Some patients required open reimplantation, regardless of the injected substance.

prevention: Exercise caution when performing bilateral RALUR because transient urinary retention may occur.

toxicities.incidence: De novo hydronephrosis occurs in up to 30% of cases after extravesical RALUR; the rate is described as similar after open ureteral reimplantation.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Initially give CAP to every symptomatic patient diagnosed within the first year of life, irrespective of reflux grade or focal uptake defects on a radionuclide scan.
prophylaxis.target_population: Symptomatic patients diagnosed within the first year of life

prophylaxis.recommendation: CAP is an initial treatment option for children with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR. Reserve surgical care for CAP noncompliance, breakthrough febrile UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting during long-term follow-up.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR

prophylaxis.recommendation: For symptomatic toilet-trained patients with high-grade reflux, abnormal kidneys, and LUTD, treat LUTD first alongside CAP. The risk-category table also specifies initial LUTD treatment with CAP for symptomatic toilet-trained patients with high-grade reflux and normal kidneys who have LUTD.
prophylaxis.target_population: Symptomatic toilet-trained patients with high-grade reflux and LUTD in the specified risk categories

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use CAP as initial treatment for symptomatic patients before toilet training who have high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys, and for asymptomatic patients with high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys identified through prenatal hydronephrosis or a sibling with VUR.
prophylaxis.target_population: The specified moderate-risk patients with high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys

prophylaxis.recommendation: CAP is an option alongside initial LUTD treatment for symptomatic patients with normal kidneys, low-grade reflux, and LUTD; it is also an alternative to no treatment for symptomatic patients with normal kidneys, low-grade reflux, and no LUTD. For asymptomatic patients with normal kidneys and low-grade reflux, the risk-category table lists no treatment or CAP in infants. Children with lower-grade reflux and no symptoms should be offered close surveillance without antibiotic prophylaxis.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with low-grade reflux in the specified risk categories

prophylaxis.recommendation: A practical approach is to consider continuing CAP until BBD resolves, although reliable evidence defining CAP duration in VUR is unavailable. Recommendations described in the literature generally use a daily antibiotic dose of a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose; commonly used agents are Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ), amoxicillin, and nitrofurantoin.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children with VUR receiving CAP, particularly those with BBD
prophylaxis.duration: Until BBD resolution may be considered; the literature does not establish a reliable duration.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Intermittent antibiotic prophylaxis is listed among conservative management options.
Circumcision may be considered during early infancy as part of conservative management; the stated basis is its effectiveness in reducing infection risk in normal children.
prophylaxis.target_population: Male infants considered for conservative management

infection_management.prevention: CAP may be used according to VUR risk, and BBD or LUTD should be assessed and treated when present. In children receiving CAP who develop a breakthrough febrile UTI, a change to another prophylactic antibiotic may be considered; an available antibiogram can inform the choice.
infection_management.management: Provide immediate parenteral antibiotics. Breakthrough febrile infection despite prophylaxis warrants abandoning conservative management and considering intervention; reimplantation or endoscopic correction should be offered for frequent breakthrough infections.

infection_management.prevention: Evaluate children presenting with UTI for BBD and manage it before treating VUR. CAP can reduce recurrence in selected patients, but is not required for every patient with VUR; trials found no or minimal benefit in low-grade reflux.
infection_management.management: In children with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR, initial medical treatment can be considered, with surgery reserved for CAP noncompliance, febrile breakthrough infections despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting during long-term follow-up.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Febrile UTI associated with antenatal hydronephrosis and presumed or confirmed VUR
infection_management.prevention: CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with a history of febrile UTI in this setting. Whether infants whose asymptomatic VUR is found during the antenatal hydronephrosis work-up benefit from CAP remains uncertain.
Management of VUR aims to preserve kidney function by reducing the risk of pyelonephritis.

therapies_index.name: watchful waiting
approved_indications: A conservative option for children with VUR; close observation without antibiotic prophylaxis is offered to children with asymptomatic lower-grade reflux.
monitoring: Individualised follow-up may include renal and bladder US, height and weight, blood pressure, and possibly serum creatinine.

therapies_index.name: intermittent antibiotic prophylaxis
approved_indications: Listed as a conservative treatment option for VUR.

therapies_index.name: CAP
approved_indications: Initial treatment for symptomatic VUR diagnosed during the first year of life, irrespective of reflux grade or focal uptake defects on a radionuclide scan.
An initial medical option for children with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR.
An initial treatment in several risk groups with high-grade reflux or LUTD; its use should be selective because it is not necessary for every patient with VUR.

May prevent further febrile UTIs in children with prior febrile UTIs and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR. Benefit for infants whose VUR is asymptomatic and discovered during evaluation of antenatal hydronephrosis remains uncertain.
therapies_index.administration: Literature recommendations generally describe daily antibiotics at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose. A practical approach is to continue CAP until BBD resolves, although its optimal duration is not established.
key_toxicities: The PREDICT trial reported more non-Escherichia coli organisms and antibiotic resistance among infants receiving CAP.
The RIVUR study associated prophylaxis with increased antimicrobial resistance.
monitoring: Surveillance and decisions about stopping CAP should be individualised, taking account of febrile UTI and access to care.
Routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children.

therapies_index.name: TMP-SMZ
approved_indications: One of the antibiotics most commonly used for CAP in children with VUR.
therapies_index.administration: For CAP, literature recommendations generally use daily antibiotics at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose.
key_toxicities: Risk of hepatic injury in infants aged <6 wk.
Potential kidney toxicity in children with severe renal insufficiency.
monitoring: In the RIVUR study, TMP-SMZ prophylaxis for 2 yr was not associated with adverse effects on complete blood count, serum electrolytes, or creatinine; routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children.

therapies_index.name: amoxicillin
approved_indications: One of the antibiotics most commonly used for CAP in children with VUR.
therapies_index.administration: For CAP, literature recommendations generally use daily antibiotics at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose.

therapies_index.name: nitrofurantoin
approved_indications: One of the antibiotics most commonly used for CAP in children with VUR.
therapies_index.administration: For CAP, literature recommendations generally use daily antibiotics at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose.
key_toxicities: Risk of haemolytic anaemia before the age of 4 mo.

therapies_index.name: parenteral antibiotic treatment
approved_indications: Immediate treatment of febrile breakthrough infections.

therapies_index.name: bladder and bowel rehabilitation
approved_indications: Conservative management for children with VUR and LUTD; bladder and bowel dysfunction should be managed before treating VUR.
monitoring: Assess LUTD and febrile UTI during follow-up.

therapies_index.name: urotherapy
approved_indications: Treatment of LUTD in children with VUR; persistent LUTD despite urotherapy may prompt consideration of an intervention.
monitoring: Reassess LUTD and kidney status after successful urotherapy.

therapies_index.name: circumcision
approved_indications: May be considered during early infancy as part of conservative management of VUR; the cited evidence for reducing infection risk concerns normal children.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic subureteric injection of bulking agents
approved_indications: An alternative to long-term antibiotic prophylaxis or open surgery for childhood VUR.
Endoscopic correction may be offered for lower reflux grades or frequent breakthrough infections; it cannot be recommended for every infant with high-grade reflux.
therapies_index.administration: Bulking material is injected endoscopically beneath the ureter.
key_toxicities: Acquired VUJO may occur during long-term follow-up; late obstruction is a concern in patients with high-grade reflux and dilated ureters.
monitoring: Follow-up should account for possible delayed VUJO; short-term assessment at 3–6 mo alone does not establish the long-term obstruction rate.

therapies_index.name: polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE or Teflon)
therapies_index.administration: Previously used as a material for endoscopic injection; it is not approved for use in children.

therapies_index.name: dextranomer/hyaluronic acid (D/HA; Deflux, Dexell)
approved_indications: A commonly used material for endoscopic injection to correct VUR.
key_toxicities: Early and delayed obstruction after Deflux injection was reported for <1% of patients.
monitoring: Follow-up for ureteral obstruction, including delayed obstruction.

therapies_index.name: polyacrylate-polyalcohol copolymer (PPC) hydrogel (Vantris)
approved_indications: A commonly used material for endoscopic injection to correct VUR.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic injection; the volume needed for a comparable success rate is generally lower for PPC than for D/HA.
key_toxicities: Longer-term studies have reported higher VUJO rates with PPC; higher obstruction rates have continued to be observed despite ureteric fibrosis and inflammatory changes similar to those seen with other injected materials.
monitoring: Follow-up for VUJO, including late obstruction.

therapies_index.name: double-J stenting
approved_indications: Temporary treatment that resolved most reported cases of obstruction following endoscopic VUR correction.

therapies_index.name: ureteral reimplantation
therapies_index.mechanism: Most described techniques lengthen the intramural ureter by embedding it beneath the mucosa.
approved_indications: Surgical correction of VUR, particularly persistent high-grade reflux; reimplantation or endoscopic correction may be offered for frequent breakthrough infections.
An option for obstruction following endoscopic correction when temporary double-J stenting does not suffice.
therapies_index.administration: Open or minimally invasive approaches are described.

therapies_index.name: open ureteral reimplantation (OUR)
therapies_index.mechanism: Most described reimplantation techniques lengthen the intramural ureter by embedding it beneath the mucosa.
approved_indications: Open surgical correction of paediatric VUR.

therapies_index.name: laparoscopic extravesical ureteral reimplantation (LEVUR)
approved_indications: A surgical option for VUR that is generally preferred for unilateral low-grade cases; laparoscopic surgery is not recommended as a routine procedure but may be offered as an alternative in experienced centres.

therapies_index.name: transvesicoscopic ureteral reimplantation (TVUR)
approved_indications: A surgical option for VUR; laparoscopic surgery is not recommended as a routine procedure but may be offered as an alternative in experienced centres.

therapies_index.name: robot-assisted laparoscopic ureteral reimplantation (RALUR)
approved_indications: A feasible surgical option for primary paediatric VUR.
Older children with complex anatomy or a previous failed injection or open reimplantation could benefit from the exposure afforded by a robotic approach.
therapies_index.administration: Most commonly performed through an extravesical approach; unilateral or bilateral surgery is possible.
key_toxicities: Bilateral procedures carry a risk of transient urinary retention.
De novo hydronephrosis can occur in up to 30% of cases after extravesical RALUR and resolves without intervention in the overwhelming majority.
A cited systematic review found more postoperative complications requiring secondary intervention with RALUR than with OUR.

therapies_index.name: nephrectomy
approved_indications: May be an option for children with recurrent febrile UTIs and hypofunctioning renal units.

conditions.name: vesicoureteral reflux
conditions.description: Reflux of urine up the urinary tract in children. Management aims to preserve kidney function by reducing the risk of pyelonephritis. Recurrent infections associated with VUR can lead to renal scarring, although VUR alone does not cause postnatal renal damage.
conditions.epidemiology: Among infants screened because of prenatally identified hydronephrosis, VUR prevalence was 16.2% (7–35%). Siblings of children with VUR had a 27.4% (3–51%) risk of VUR, while offspring of affected parents had an incidence of 35.7% (21.2–61.4%). Among children with febrile UTIs, VUR was more frequent in boys than girls (29% vs 14%).
conditions.clinical_presentation: VUR may be identified after prenatal hydronephrosis, during evaluation of febrile UTI, or in relatives of affected patients. It may be asymptomatic or occur with recurrent febrile UTIs, LUTD or BBD. A focal uptake defect on a radionuclide scan is present in 10–40% of children with symptomatic VUR and may reflect congenital dysplasia, acquired postinfectious injury, or both.

subtypes.name: primary VUR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An anatomical, functional or physiological disorder.

subtypes.name: secondary VUR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Reflux arising from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic bladder dysfunction; it often affects both sides.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical assessment of height, weight, blood pressure, febrile UTI, and bladder and bowel function
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess general development, infection history and functional factors relevant to management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During the diagnostic evaluation of children with VUR.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: LUTD and BBD are relevant to infection risk and should be assessed particularly after toilet training.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation; serum creatinine may also be monitored during conservative follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the kidneys and bladder, provide initial imaging after birth or febrile UTI, and monitor renal growth and status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As the initial postnatal test following prenatal hydronephrosis, deferred until the first week after birth because of neonatal oliguria; as initial imaging after a febrile UTI and during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal postnatal study does not exclude VUR. Bladder wall thickness or configuration may indirectly suggest bladder outlet obstruction and VUR. Abnormal renal findings during febrile infection indicate higher VUR risk and warrant VCUG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose and grade VUR and assess bladder and urethral configuration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly for initial VUR evaluation; for children with febrile infection and abnormal renal US; after cortical abnormalities are identified by DMSA in neonates or infants with prenatal hydronephrosis; and, in antenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis, for selected findings including bilateral high-grade hydronephrosis, duplex kidneys with hydronephrosis, a solitary kidney with hydronephrosis, ureterocele, ureteric dilatation, abnormal bladders or a history of febrile UTIs.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The conventional examination remains the diagnostic reference standard for grading reflux. Images can also identify intrarenal reflux, which is associated with greater renal scarring risk. A standardised examination protocol should be used.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide another means of diagnosing VUR and detecting intrarenal reflux.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As an alternative diagnostic imaging option to VCUG.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide an alternative imaging modality for VUR evaluation.
Provide an alternative imaging modality for VUR evaluation.
Visualise renal cortical tissue and assess differential function between the kidneys; when appropriately timed, assess renal scarring.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When available after VUR diagnosis, or near a febrile UTI as the initial test in a considered top-down evaluation, followed by VCUG if renal involvement is identified.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A focal cortical uptake defect can reflect congenital or acquired injury. In the top-down approach, evidence of acute pyelonephritis or cortical abnormality determines whether VCUG follows.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate bladder dysfunction and suspected secondary reflux.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When secondary VUR is suspected, including severe neurogenic bladder dysfunction or boys with VCUG findings suggestive of posterior urethral valves; also when standard LUTD therapy fails.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to a predictive score for VUR after a first febrile UTI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing VUR risk after a child's first febrile UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document lists white blood cell count ( 15 000/ml) alongside age (>6 mo), sepsis and abnormal renal US as potential score inputs; it does not state a comparison sign for the count.

definitions.description: Reflux remains below the renal pelvis; ureteral dilatation can vary in degree.
Reflux extends into the renal pelvis without collecting-system dilatation; the fornices retain their normal appearance.
The ureter is mildly or moderately dilated and may kink; collecting-system dilatation is moderate, while the fornices are normal or only minimally altered.
The ureter and collecting system show moderate dilatation, with possible ureteral kinking; the fornices are blunted, but papillary impressions remain visible.
The ureter is markedly dilated and kinked, with pronounced collecting-system dilatation; papillary impressions are no longer visible, and intraparenchymal reflux is described.

staging.additional_rules: The five grades are assigned using VCUG. The document describes grades I–III as lower-grade reflux and grades IV–V as high-grade reflux in its management discussion.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Described as a practical aid when deciding on further treatment, surveillance, prophylaxis or surgery; its inputs and categories are not specified.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Described as a practical aid when deciding on further treatment, surveillance, prophylaxis or surgery; its inputs and categories are not specified.

prognostic_tools.name: Management and follow-up according to risk category
components: Prenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis or an affected sibling

risk_groups.criteria: Symptomatic patients after toilet training with high-grade reflux (grade IV–V), abnormal kidneys and LUTD.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The document indicates a greater likelihood of earlier intervention.

risk_groups.criteria: Symptomatic patients after toilet training with high-grade reflux (grade IV–V), abnormal kidneys and no LUTD.
Symptomatic patients before toilet training with high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Spontaneous resolution is described as more frequent in males.

risk_groups.criteria: Asymptomatic patients with PNH or an affected sibling, high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys.
Symptomatic patients after toilet training with high-grade reflux, normal kidneys and LUTD.
Symptomatic patients after toilet training with low-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys, with or without LUTD.
Symptomatic patients with normal kidneys, low-grade reflux and LUTD.
Symptomatic patients with normal kidneys, low-grade reflux and no LUTD.
Asymptomatic patients with normal kidneys and low-grade reflux.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The categories guide initial management and follow-up. Other factors considered in selecting management include focal uptake defects, clinical course, ipsilateral renal function, bilaterality, associated urinary tract anomalies, age, sex, adherence and parental preference.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up is individualised because no optimal interval or frequency is established. The risk categories specify full re-evaluation after 6 mo for high-risk patients with LUTD and after 12–24 mo for symptomatic patients before toilet training or asymptomatic patients with high-grade reflux and abnormal kidneys. Other categories call for monitoring through or beyond puberty, after successful urotherapy, or for febrile UTI and LUTD as appropriate.
recommended_tests: Renal and bladder US to assess renal status and growth
Assessment for febrile UTI and LUTD
Postoperative VCUG only when indicated in the specified high-risk group without LUTD
long_term_effects: Renal scarring may follow recurrent infection.
In follow-up studies, 10–20% of children with a focal uptake defect on a radionuclide scan developed hypertension or end-stage renal disease.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Spontaneous resolution varies with age at presentation, sex, grade, laterality, clinical presentation and anatomy. Resolution was nearly 80% for grades I and II and 30–50% for grades III–V within 4– 5 yr of follow-up. Bilateral high-grade reflux resolves less often; cortical abnormalities, bladder dysfunction and breakthrough febrile UTIs predict poorer resolution.

conditions.name: primary VUR
conditions.description: An anatomical, functional or physiological form of VUR with potentially serious renal and cardiovascular consequences.
conditions.epidemiology: Primary VUR has an incidence of nearly 1% in children.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It can be identified in children with febrile UTI or prenatal hydronephrosis and may coexist with BBD. Possible consequences include focal uptake defects on radionuclide imaging, hypertension and renal failure.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For initial assessment when VUR evaluation is warranted.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reflux is classified into five grades under the International Reflux Study Committee system.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate renal and bladder findings and monitor renal growth.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Following prenatal hydronephrosis or febrile UTI, and during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal result does not exclude VUR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess cortical abnormalities, renal scarring and differential kidney function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When available after VUR diagnosis or as part of a considered top-down evaluation after febrile UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A focal uptake defect can indicate congenital dysplasia, acquired postinfectious damage or both.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify coexisting dysfunction relevant to recurrent infection and treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In children with UTI or VUR, especially after toilet training.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Coexisting BBD and VUR doubles the risk of UTI recurrence.

definitions.description: Reflux does not extend to the renal pelvis; ureteral dilatation varies.
Reflux reaches the renal pelvis without collecting-system dilatation or fornix alteration.
Mild or moderate ureteral dilatation, with possible kinking, accompanies moderate collecting-system dilatation and normal or minimally changed fornices.
Moderate ureteral and collecting-system dilatation occurs with possible ureteral kinking and blunted fornices; papillary impressions remain visible.
Marked ureteral dilatation and kinking occur with pronounced collecting-system dilatation, loss of visible papillary impressions and intraparenchymal reflux.

prognostic_tools.name: Boston’s Children Hospital VUR Resolution Rate Calculator
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The document identifies it as an aid to decisions about surveillance, prophylaxis and intervention but does not describe its inputs.

prognostic_tools.name: iReflux Risk Calculator
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The document identifies it as an aid to decisions about surveillance, prophylaxis and intervention but does not describe its inputs.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up is tailored to the child; the document establishes no uniform timing or frequency.
recommended_tests: Assessment for febrile UTI and bladder and bowel dysfunction
long_term_effects: Focal renal defects may be followed by hypertension or end-stage renal disease.
Recurrent infection associated with VUR can cause renal scarring.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Spontaneous resolution is more likely with presentation at age <1 yr, grade I–III reflux, or asymptomatic presentation after prenatal hydronephrosis or identification of an affected sibling. Renal cortical abnormalities, bladder dysfunction and breakthrough febrile UTIs predict less favourable resolution.

conditions.name: secondary VUR
conditions.description: VUR caused by bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Reflux frequently occurs bilaterally. Its grade may increase with rising bladder pressure from outlet obstruction or with neurological deterioration affecting the bladder.

subtypes.name: bladder outlet obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Obstruction can increase bladder pressure and is described as a cause of secondary VUR.

subtypes.name: neurogenic bladder dysfunction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Deterioration of neurogenic bladder function can be associated with a higher reflux grade.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected secondary VUR and severe bladder dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When secondary VUR is suspected, including severe neurogenic bladder dysfunction or boys whose VCUG suggests posterior urethral valves.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and grade reflux and assess bladder and urethral configuration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic evaluation of suspected VUR.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In boys, findings suggestive of posterior urethral valves support further evaluation with video-urodynamic studies.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of standard VUR imaging.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Bladder wall thickness and configuration may indirectly suggest bladder outlet obstruction and VUR.

definitions.description: Reflux remains below the renal pelvis, with variable ureteral dilatation.
Reflux reaches the renal pelvis without dilatation of the collecting system; fornices remain normal.
The ureter shows mild or moderate dilatation, sometimes with kinking; the collecting system is moderately dilated and fornices are normal or minimally altered.
The ureter and collecting system are moderately dilated, with possible ureteral kinking; blunted fornices still show papillary impressions.
Severe ureteral dilatation and kinking accompany pronounced collecting-system dilatation, absent visible papillary impressions and intraparenchymal reflux.

staging.additional_rules: The document applies the five-grade VCUG classification to VUR without specifying a different system for secondary VUR.

follow_up.schedule: The document does not specify a separate follow-up interval for secondary VUR; VUR follow-up is individualised.

recommendations.statement: ceVUS may be used as another diagnostic option for VUR besides VCUG.
Tell parents of children with VUR that VUR is prevalent among siblings and offspring.
recommendations.context: Counselling families of children with VUR

recommendations.statement: Start CAP in every symptomatic patient diagnosed during the first year of life, irrespective of reflux grade or the presence of focal uptake defects on a radionuclide scan.
recommendations.context: Initial treatment after diagnosis during the first year of life

recommendations.statement: Treat febrile breakthrough infections promptly with parenteral antibiotics.
Use medical treatment initially for every child presenting at age 1–5 yr.
Closely monitor asymptomatic children with lower grades of reflux without giving antibiotic prophylaxis.
Assess every child thoroughly for LUTD, particularly after toilet training; when LUTD is present, treat it first.
recommendations.context: Assessment and initial treatment of LUTD

recommendations.statement: Offer ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic correction to patients who have frequent breakthrough infections.
Offer reimplantation for persistent high-grade reflux and endoscopic correction for lower reflux grades.
recommendations.context: Selection of a corrective procedure by reflux grade

recommendations.statement: Offer surgical repair to children older than 1 yr who have high-grade reflux and abnormal renal parenchyma.
recommendations.context: High-grade reflux with abnormal renal parenchyma

recommendations.statement: Offer surgical correction when parents prefer definitive treatment over conservative management.

Choose management according to focal uptake defects on a radionuclide scan, clinical course, reflux grade, ipsilateral renal function, bilaterality, bladder function, associated urinary tract anomalies, age and sex, compliance, and parental preference; use Table 4 for risk factors and follow-up.
Use a more aggressive multidisciplinary approach for high-risk patients who already have renal impairment.
recommendations.context: High-risk patients with established renal impairment

recommendations.statement: Use VCUG to evaluate antenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis when US shows bilateral high-grade hydronephrosis, duplex kidneys with hydronephrosis, a solitary kidney with hydronephrosis, ureterocele, ureteric dilatation, or an abnormal bladder, or when there is a history of febrile UTIs.
recommendations.rationale: The likelihood of VUR is higher with these findings.

recommendations.statement: Do not use VCUG for infants with minimal prenatal renal pelvic dilatation and no postnatal calicectasis.
recommendations.context: Infants with minimal prenatal renal pelvic dilatation
recommendations.rationale: VUR is uncommon in this group and is likely to be low grade when present.
recommendations.source_heading: 3.2.1. Infants presenting with prenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis

rows: Grade I

artifacts.title: Evidence summary for managing vesicoureteric reflux in childhood

rows: Evidence does not show a significant benefit from correcting persistent, asymptomatic low-grade reflux (grades I–III) when the kidneys are normal. The traditional sequence of initial medical treatment followed by intervention for breakthrough infection and a new focal uptake defect on a radionuclide scan warrants reconsideration in favour of treatment tailored to risk groups.

Consider surgical correction for persistent high-grade reflux (grades IV/V). There is no consensus on when to operate or which correction to use. Reimplantation has better outcomes than endoscopic correction at higher reflux grades, while endoscopic injection can produce satisfactory results at lower grades.

Management selection depends on focal uptake defects on a radionuclide scan, clinical course, reflux grade, ipsilateral renal function, bilaterality, bladder function, associated urinary tract anomalies, age, compliance and parental preference. Febrile UTI, high-grade reflux, bilaterality and cortical abnormalities are risk factors for possible renal damage; LUTD additionally raises the risk of a new focal uptake defect on a radionuclide scan.

special_populations.considerations: Kidney and bladder US is the standard initial postnatal assessment, but it should be deferred until the first week after birth because neonates can have early oliguria. A normal postnatal US does not rule out VUR. Cortical abnormalities on DMSA warrant VCUG. The panel recommends VCUG when antenatal hydronephrosis is accompanied by bilateral high-grade hydronephrosis, duplex kidneys with hydronephrosis, a solitary kidney with hydronephrosis, ureterocele, ureteric dilatation, an abnormal bladder, or a history of febrile UTIs. VUR is uncommon with minimal prenatal renal pelvic dilatation and no postnatal calicectasis; when present, it is likely to be low grade.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: VCUG is not recommended for infants with minimal prenatal renal pelvic dilatation and no postnatal calicectasis. CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with previous febrile UTIs and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR; whether it benefits infants whose VUR is asymptomatic remains uncertain.

special_populations.population: Siblings and offspring of children with VUR
special_populations.considerations: Siblings of children with VUR have a 27.4% (3–51%) risk of VUR; offspring of parents with VUR have a 35.7% (21.2–61.4%) incidence. Screening asymptomatic siblings and offspring remains controversial, and the available evidence does not support screening all of them. Families should be told about the increased likelihood of VUR and taught to recognise UTI symptoms.

Renal US should be the initial assessment and should also be used during follow-up to assess renal growth. Children with febrile infection and an abnormal renal US have a higher risk of VUR. An initial DMSA scan close to the infection, followed by VCUG when kidney involvement is found, is a strategy that could especially be considered in children aged >1 yr because VCUG is invasive. In an analysis using RIVUR and CUTIE data, this strategy was associated with more subsequent recurrent febrile UTIs and a risk of missed VUR diagnoses, but significantly less VCUG and CAP use than a VCUG-first strategy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Children with febrile infection and abnormal renal US findings should be assessed for VUR with VCUG. A breakthrough febrile infection calls for immediate parenteral antibiotics. When a febrile UTI breaks through prophylaxis, changing the prophylactic antibiotic may be considered, guided by an antibiogram if available.

special_populations.population: Toilet-trained children with BBD or LUTD
special_populations.considerations: BBD is common among toilet-trained children with UTI, whether or not they have primary VUR. Children with both BBD and VUR have twice the risk of UTI recurrence; those with both LUTD and VUR are at greater risk of recurrent febrile UTIs than children with VUR alone. VUR accompanied by LUTD is suggested to resolve faster once LUTD is corrected. LUTD with febrile UTIs warrants careful assessment with US and VCUG.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Children presenting with UTIs should be evaluated for BBD and managed accordingly before VUR treatment. If LUTD is present, its treatment should come first. A child whose LUTD does not respond to standard treatment should undergo video-urodynamic investigation. A practical approach is to continue CAP until BBD resolves, although reliable evidence on CAP duration is lacking.

special_populations.considerations: Secondary VUR arises from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic bladder dysfunction and often occurs bilaterally. Its grade may correlate with increased bladder pressure or deterioration associated with neurogenic bladder.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Video-urodynamic studies are important when secondary VUR is suspected, including in children with severe neurogenic bladder dysfunction or boys whose VCUG suggests posterior urethral valves.

special_populations.population: Children with high-grade VUR and febrile UTI
special_populations.considerations: Febrile UTI and high-grade reflux are risk factors for possible renal damage. Spontaneous resolution is less likely with bilateral high-grade reflux, renal cortical abnormalities, bladder dysfunction, or breakthrough febrile UTIs.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Initial medical treatment can be considered. Surgical care is reserved for CAP noncompliance, breakthrough febrile UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR that persists during long-term follow-up. Surgical repair should be offered to children above the age of 1 yr who have high-grade reflux and abnormal renal parenchyma.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children selected for endoscopic correction, particularly those with lower-grade reflux.
decision_rules: Offer endoscopic correction for lower reflux grades.
Use reflux timing during VCUG when assessing likely treatment success: reflux confined to voiding has a higher success rate than reflux occurring during filling.
Consider the risk of later VUJO, particularly with high-grade reflux and dilated ureters.

recommended_regimens.name: Endoscopic subureteric injection of bulking agents
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer endoscopic correction for lower-grade VUR; D/HA and PPC are the bulking materials described as most commonly used.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A meta-analysis of 5527 patients and 8101 renal units reported reflux resolution by ureter after one treatment of 78.5% for grade I and II reflux, 72% for grade III, 63% for grade IV, and 51% for grade V. Success after a second treatment was 68%, after a third treatment 34%, and after one or more injections 85%.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Repeat injection may be considered if an earlier injection fails; the guideline reports results after a first, second, and third treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Ureteral reimplantation
alternative_regimens.summary: Surgical correction has better results than endoscopic correction for higher reflux grades.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent high-grade VUR or individualized choice of definitive intervention.

not_recommended.name: PTFE
not_recommended.reason: Not approved for children because of concerns about particle migration.

not_recommended.name: Endoscopic treatment for every child with high-grade reflux
not_recommended.reason: The guideline does not recommend universal endoscopic treatment because not all high-grade cases are symptomatic.

response_assessment.method: Assess reflux resolution and possible VUJO, including delayed obstruction.
response_assessment.interpretation: Short-term success and VUJO rates appear comparable across bulking agents, while longer-term reports claim a higher VUJO rate with PPC.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The meta-analysis reported lower success for duplicate (50%) than single (73%) systems and for neuropathic (62%) than normal (74%) bladders. Early and delayed obstruction after Deflux injection was reported for <1% of patients. Most obstruction cases resolved after temporary double-J stenting, although some required open reimplantation. Evidence for an added benefit over CAP alone remains uncertain because the available studies are few and methodologically limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children undergoing ureteral reimplantation for whom a minimally invasive approach is being considered.
decision_rules: Consider laparoscopic surgery as an alternative in centers with established experience, not as a routine procedure.
LEVUR is generally preferred for unilateral low-grade cases.
Consider RALUR for older children with complex anatomy or after failed injection or open reimplantation; use caution for bilateral RALUR.

alternative_regimens.name: LEVUR
alternative_regimens.summary: A minimally invasive reimplantation option; a cited comparison found that LEVUR and TVUR both provided favorable resolution and complication outcomes.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Generally preferred for unilateral low-grade cases in an experienced center.

alternative_regimens.name: TVUR
alternative_regimens.summary: A minimally invasive reimplantation option with favorable resolution and complication outcomes in the cited comparison with LEVUR.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualized selection in an experienced center.

alternative_regimens.name: RALUR
alternative_regimens.summary: A feasible robotic approach for primary paediatric VUR, with success reported as similar to OUR; the extravesical approach is most commonly used.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be useful for older children with complex anatomy or following failed injection or open reimplantation.

alternative_regimens.name: OUR
alternative_regimens.summary: Open reimplantation is an established surgical comparator to robotic reimplantation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualized choice of surgical approach.

not_recommended.name: Routine laparoscopic approach
not_recommended.reason: Potential advantages over open surgery remain under evaluation, so the guideline does not recommend routine use.

response_assessment.method: Assess surgical success and complications, including urinary retention and new hydronephrosis.
response_assessment.interpretation: Bilateral RALUR carries a risk of transient urinary retention. De novo hydronephrosis after extravesical RALUR can occur in up to 30% of cases and resolves spontaneously in the overwhelming majority.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited systematic review found higher operative times, costs, and postoperative complications requiring secondary intervention with RALUR than with OUR, but less postoperative pain and shorter hospital stay.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with recurrent febrile UTIs and hypofunctioning renal units.
decision_rules: Nephrectomy may be an option when recurrent febrile infections coexist with a hypofunctioning renal unit.

alternative_regimens.name: Nephrectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered as a surgical option for a poorly functioning renal unit in a child with recurrent febrile UTIs.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Recurrent febrile UTIs and a hypofunctioning renal unit.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This article summarises the 2023 update to the EAU/ESPU guidance on VUR in children. It addresses diagnostic evaluation and management using patient risk to guide the selection of tests and interventions.

document_sections.heading: Background and objective
document_sections.content: Prescriptive evidence for VUR remains limited, and the overall evidence level is low. The guidance aims to offer a practical, risk-based approach to treatment and to the selective use of diagnostic tests and interventions.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors undertook a structured review of relevant publications issued since the preceding update and through March 2022.

document_sections.heading: Key findings and limitations
document_sections.content: BBD frequently occurs in toilet-trained children with UTI, whether or not they have primary VUR, and raises the risks of febrile UTI and focal defects on radionuclide imaging. CAP is not necessarily needed for every patient with VUR. Its optimal duration is not reliably established; continuing it until BBD resolves is a practical approach. For children with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR, initial medical care is an option, while surgery is reserved for nonadherence to CAP, febrile breakthrough UTI despite CAP, or symptomatic reflux persisting during long-term follow-up. Comparisons of laparoscopic extravesical and transvesicoscopic ureteral reimplantation found both suitable regarding reflux resolution and complications. Extravesical surgery is the predominant robotic reimplantation approach, although techniques and reported success vary substantially.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions and clinical implications
document_sections.content: The updated 2023 EAU/ESPU guidance offers practical considerations for diagnosing and managing childhood VUR.

document_sections.heading: Advancing practice
document_sections.content: BBD should be treated when it occurs in a child with VUR. Continuing CAP until BBD has resolved is suggested as a practical approach to its duration.

document_sections.heading: Patient summary
document_sections.content: The article updates guidance on diagnosing and treating childhood urinary reflux, in which urine travels backward through the urinary tract. Addressing bladder and bowel dysfunction is important because it commonly accompanies UTI in toilet-trained children.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: The guidance seeks to support practical VUR treatment through risk assessment and selective indications for investigations and interventions. The panel cautions that overly simple rules would fail to reflect the complexity of VUR, which can arise from many underlying causes. This article summarises the 2023 update to the EAU and ESPU paediatric VUR chapter. A shortage of robust prospective randomised controlled trials limits the strength of management guidance. The VUR literature is generally sparse and provides low-level evidence; most studies are retrospective, combine heterogeneous patients, and stratify quality poorly. Consequently, recommendations for children with VUR cannot be grounded in high-quality studies.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: EAU/ESPU paediatric urology chapters undergo periodic updating every 4 yr, and an earlier summary appeared in 2012. For this VUR update, a librarian conducted a structured search for relevant work published from the previous update in June 2018 through March 2022; at least two panel members reviewed it. Eligibility was restricted to English-language publications. The sources were MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews via Ovid. Searches combined MeSH terms and free-text terms concerning VUR and reflux in paediatric patients with Boolean operators and included root-word variants. Conference abstracts were excluded.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results
document_sections.content: The results address the epidemiology and mechanisms of VUR, diagnostic evaluation, nonsurgical care, and surgical treatment.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Epidemiology, aetiology, and pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Primary VUR involves anatomical and/or functional or physiological abnormalities and can have serious consequences, including focal defects on radionuclide imaging, hypertension, and renal failure. Genetic studies have identified monogenic causes and significant differences in genes involved in innate immunity and epithelial function between children with VUR/febrile UTIs and controls. Secondary VUR results from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic bladder dysfunction; it is often bilateral, and reflux grade may track increases in bladder pressure from obstruction or neuropathological progression in a neurogenic bladder. Primary VUR has an incidence of nearly 1% in children. Among infants screened after prenatal US identified hydronephrosis, VUR prevalence was 16.2% (7–35%). The risk was 27.4% (3–51%) among siblings of affected children, while incidence among offspring of affected parents was 35.7% (21.2–61.4%). Febrile UTIs occur more often in girls because of anatomical differences, but boys with febrile UTIs are more likely than girls with febrile UTIs to have VUR (29% vs 14%). VUR alone does not cause postnatal renal damage; recurrent infections accompanying it can produce renal scarring. Focal defects on radionuclide scans occur in 10–40% of children with symptomatic VUR and can reflect congenital dysplasia and/or acquired postinfectious injury. Congenital renal injury is attributed to disturbed kidney development secondary to substantial bladder disease. Injury acquired after pyelonephritis is thought to involve interacting host and bacterial factors, potentially causing acute functional changes and permanent scars, with possible adverse effects on growth and general wellbeing. A focal radionuclide uptake defect is an important risk factor for febrile breakthrough UTI and may identify patients at risk of persistent symptomatic VUR. Spontaneous resolution depends on age at presentation, sex, reflux grade, laterality, mode of presentation, and anatomy such as duplex systems or an ectopic ureter. More rapid resolution is likely with presentation at age <1 yr, grade I–III reflux, or asymptomatic presentation following prenatal hydronephrosis or identification of an affected sibling. Within 4– 5 yr of follow-up, resolution is nearly 80% for grades I and II and 30–50% for grades III–V; bilateral high-grade reflux resolves spontaneously less often. Several Scandinavian studies reported complete resolution of >25% in high-grade VUR. Renal cortical abnormalities, bladder dysfunction, and febrile breakthrough UTIs predict poorer resolution. Higher reflux grades tend to accompany more focal radionuclide uptake defects. Such defects occur in 10% of patients with prenatal hydronephrosis and may occur in as many as 30% of those with LUTD. Follow-up studies found that 10–20% of children with a focal radionuclide uptake defect develop hypertension or end-stage renal disease. LUTD and VUR commonly coexist, sometimes alongside bowel dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Evaluation should cover general health and development, including height, weight, and blood pressure; febrile UTI; renal status, including serum creatinine and GFR; reflux; and bladder and bowel function. Standard imaging comprises renal and bladder US, VCUG, and nuclear renal scans. VCUG is the standard initial diagnostic method for VUR, which the International Reflux Study Committee classifies into five grades; Table 1 provides the grading criteria. Few studies have assessed diagnostic radiation exposure accurately or comparatively. Differences in VCUG fluoroscopy protocols, imaging equipment, and radionuclide exposure in children with reduced kidney function contribute to conflicting dose assessments. ceVUS, magnetic resonance VCUG, and nuclear cystography are alternative imaging options. Despite its invasiveness and ionising radiation, conventional VCUG remains the diagnostic reference because it better establishes reflux grade and depicts bladder and urethral configuration; its performance requires a standardised protocol. Intrarenal reflux, detectable on VCUG or ceVUS, is associated with greater renal scarring risk. DMSA is regarded as the best nuclear agent for assessing cortical tissue and differential function of the kidneys. Video-urodynamic testing is important when secondary VUR is suspected, including severe neurogenic bladder dysfunction or VCUG findings suggestive of posterior urethral valves in boys. Table 2 presents recommendations and their rating strengths.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1. Infants presenting with prenatally diagnosed hydronephrosis
document_sections.content: Renal and bladder US is the standard first postnatal assessment. Because neonates have early oliguria, US should wait until the first week after birth. A postnatal scan without hydronephrosis does not rule out VUR. Bladder wall thickness and configuration may indirectly indicate bladder outlet obstruction and reflux. In neonates or infants with prenatal hydronephrosis, cortical abnormalities detected by DMSA warrant VCUG to investigate VUR. The panel recommends VCUG after antenatal hydronephrosis when US shows bilateral high-grade hydronephrosis, duplex kidneys with hydronephrosis, a solitary kidney with hydronephrosis, ureterocele, ureteric dilatation, or an abnormal bladder, and when there is a history of febrile UTIs, because VUR is more likely in these circumstances. VCUG is not recommended for infants with minimal prenatal renal pelvic dilatation and no postnatal calicectasis: reflux is uncommon in this group and, if present, is likely low grade.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2. Siblings and offspring of reflux patients
document_sections.content: Whether to screen asymptomatic siblings and offspring is disputed, and available evidence does not support screening all of them. Families of children with VUR should instead be told that siblings and offspring have an increased likelihood of reflux and taught to recognise UTI signs and symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3. Children with febrile UTIs
document_sections.content: Renal US should be the initial investigation after febrile UTI and should remain part of follow-up to assess kidney growth. It is the safest approach because evidence defining whom to select for reflux detection is weak. Following a first febrile UTI, age (>6 mo), sepsis, white blood cell count ( 15 000/ml), and abnormal renal US can contribute to a score predicting VUR. The EAU/ESPU paediatric UTI chapter supplies a diagnostic algorithm for these children. All children with febrile infection and an abnormal renal US should undergo VCUG because their VUR risk is higher. After VUR diagnosis, subsequent evaluation has traditionally included DMSA scanning when available. Timed appropriately, DMSA can identify scarring and individual-kidney function to inform treatment. A “top-down” strategy obtains DMSA near a febrile UTI to look for acute pyelonephritis or a cortical abnormality, then performs VCUG if kidney involvement is evident; this may be particularly worth considering at age >1 yr because VCUG is invasive. The historically more common “bottom-up” strategy performs VCUG first after an initial febrile UTI. A study analysing RIVUR and CUTIE data associated the top-down strategy, relative to bottom-up evaluation, with more subsequent recurrent febrile UTIs and possible missed VUR diagnoses, but significantly less VCUG and CAP use.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4. Children with bladder and bowel dysfunction symptoms and VUR
document_sections.content: Identifying LUTD is essential when managing VUR. Resolution of reflux accompanied by LUTD has been suggested to occur faster after LUTD is corrected. Among toilet-trained children, coexisting LUTD and VUR confers greater recurrent febrile UTI risk than VUR alone. BBD is frequent in toilet-trained children with UTI, irrespective of primary VUR. Coexisting BBD and VUR has been shown to double UTI recurrence risk. Accordingly, every child presenting with UTI should be carefully assessed for BBD and managed for it before VUR treatment; effective BBD care may have an impact comparable to CAP. VUR associated with LUTD is often low grade and US is usually normal, so VCUG is not indicated in that situation. When LUTD accompanies febrile UTIs, thorough assessment with US and VCUG is warranted. A child whose LUTD does not respond to standard therapy should undergo video-urodynamic investigation.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Disease management
document_sections.content: The central goal of treatment is to protect renal function by reducing pyelonephritis risk. The best diagnostic choices, treatment choice, and treatment timing remain disputed. Management has two broad approaches: conservative medical care and surgery.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1. Nonsurgical therapy
document_sections.content: Conservative options comprise observation, intermittent antibiotic prophylaxis or CAP, and bladder and bowel rehabilitation when LUTD is present. Follow-up during conservative care includes US imaging and checks of height, weight, and blood pressure, with serum creatinine when appropriate, to assess renal status and spontaneous reflux resolution. The literature establishes no agreed optimal interval or frequency for these assessments; follow-up should be individualised. Assessment and treatment of toilet-trained children with febrile UTI belong in conservative follow-up. In infants with high-grade VUR, conservative care can be accompanied by spontaneous downgrading or resolution, although the likelihood also depends on sex, febrile breakthrough infection, focal radionuclide uptake defects, and bladder dysfunction. Boston’s Children Hospital VUR Resolution Rate Calculator and the iReflux Risk Calculator are practical tools for decisions about continued treatment, observation, prophylaxis, or surgery. Circumcision in early infancy may be considered within conservative care because it reduces infection risk in normal children. Febrile breakthrough infection despite prophylaxis calls for abandoning conservative management and considering intervention.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.1.1. CAP
document_sections.content: Many prospective studies have examined whether CAP prevents recurrent febrile UTI and focal radionuclide uptake defects. CAP is not required for every child with VUR; trials found no or minimal benefit for low-grade reflux. In PREDICT, a randomised controlled trial across 39 European centres, Morello et al. studied infants with grade III, IV, or V VUR and no prior UTI. Treating seven children for 2 yr was necessary to prevent one UTI, without differences in renal scarring, kidney function, or UTI hospitalisation. CAP gave a small but significant reduction in first UTI, alongside increases in non-Escherichia coli organisms and antibiotic resistance. Among children with VUR receiving CAP, younger age at initial febrile UTI diagnosis ( 12 mo), bilateral reflux, and BBD independently predict febrile breakthrough UTI. Toilet-trained children and those with LUTD gain more benefit from CAP. RIVUR reported a 50% reduction in recurrent febrile UTI risk with prophylaxis, but no effect on focal radionuclide uptake defects or their consequences of hypertension and renal failure; antimicrobial resistance increased. Further risk-stratified analyses of RIVUR identified uncircumcised boys, children with BBD, and those with high-grade reflux as a high-risk group deriving significant CAP benefit. Rather than using CAP uniformly, medical care should shift from prophylaxis for dilating reflux toward selective use based on risk. Relevant febrile UTI risk factors include young age, high-grade VUR, toilet-training status, LUTD, female sex, and circumcision status. Reliable evidence for CAP duration is lacking; using it until BBD resolves is a practical approach. Recommendations in the literature generally use antibiotics every day at a quarter to half of the regular therapeutic dose. Common CAP drugs are Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ), amoxicillin, and nitrofurantoin. TMP-SMZ must be avoided at age <6 wk because of hepatic injury risk and in severe renal insufficiency because of possible kidney toxicity. Nitrofurantoin is best avoided before 4 mo because of haemolytic anaemia risk. After a febrile breakthrough UTI, changing to another prophylactic antibiotic may be considered; an available antibiogram can guide the choice. Initial medical care remains an option for a child with febrile UTI and high-grade VUR. Surgery is reserved for failure to adhere to CAP, febrile breakthrough UTIs despite CAP, or symptomatic VUR persisting over long-term follow-up, including recurrent flank pain with or without febrile UTIs. The best point to stop CAP is disputed. Recurrences are more likely after CAP for <1 yr following the last febrile UTI and in bilateral VUR. Surveillance, antireflux intervention, and CAP discontinuation should be decided individually with patients and caregivers. Detailed discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives is strongly advised, taking access to care during febrile UTI into account. Long-term CAP effects concern patients, caregivers, and clinicians. In a secondary RIVUR analysis, TMP-SMZ prophylaxis for 2 yr was not associated with adverse changes in complete blood count, serum electrolytes, or creatinine; routine laboratory testing is not mandatory in otherwise healthy children. Effects of prolonged CAP on gut microbiota remain disputed and need further study. CAP can prevent new febrile UTIs in children with a febrile UTI history and antenatal hydronephrosis with presumed or confirmed VUR. Whether it also helps infants whose asymptomatic VUR is discovered while investigating antenatal hydronephrosis remains unclear.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2. Surgical therapy
document_sections.content: Surgical options include endoscopic bulking-agent injection and open or minimally invasive ureteral reimplantation. Nephrectomy may be considered for recurrent febrile UTIs when a renal unit has poor function.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2.1. Subureteric injection of bulking material
document_sections.content: Biodegradable bulking materials have made endoscopic subureteric injection an alternative to prolonged antibiotic prophylaxis and open surgery for childhood VUR. Reflux timing on VCUG helps predict injection success: reflux limited to voiding responds more often than reflux occurring during bladder filling. Previously used agents include polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE or Teflon), which is not approved for children because of concern about particle migration. Currently common agents are dextranomer/hyaluronic acid (D/HA; Deflux, Dexell) and polyacrylate-polyalcohol copolymer (PPC) hydrogel (Vantris). A meta-analysis including 5527 patients and 8101 renal units reported resolution by ureter after one injection of 78.5% for grades I and II, 72% for grade III, 63% for grade IV, and 51% for grade V. If the initial injection failed, success was 68% with a second treatment and 34% with a third; overall success after one or more injections was 85%. Success was significantly lower in duplicate (50%) than single (73%) systems and in neuropathic (62%) than normal (74%) bladders. Injection volumes needed for comparable success differ by agent and are generally lower with PPC than with D/HA. Acquired VUJO may emerge late after endoscopic correction. Obstruction appears more frequent in patients with BBD, and high-grade reflux with ureteral dilatation raises late-obstruction risk. Although agents appear comparable for success and VUJO over short-term follow-up (3–6 mo), longer-term studies have reported more VUJO with PPC. Early or delayed obstruction after Deflux injection has nevertheless been reported in <1% of patients. Most obstructions resolved with temporary double-J stenting, but some required open reimplantation regardless of injected material. Ureteric fibrosis and/or inflammatory changes after PPC injection have been shown to resemble those with other agents, while PPC has continued to show higher obstruction rates. Whether endoscopic correction adds benefit beyond CAP alone remains uncertain because the available studies are few and methodologically weak. A significant reduction in febrile UTI incidence was reported, but not a difference in symptomatic UTI or renal damage. The ureteral diameter ratio is a relatively new objective measure that appears promising for predicting clinical outcomes and endoscopic injection success. Inadequate methodologically suitable studies currently limit clinical validation of antireflux endoscopy. Tables 3 and 4 summarise management evidence, recommendations, risk categories, and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2.2. Open surgical techniques
document_sections.content: Open VUR correction can use several intravesical or extravesical methods. Their particular advantages and complications differ, but most lengthen the intramural ureter by placing it beneath the mucosa. The techniques have been reported as safe, with few complications and success rates of 92–98%. Overall, surgical approaches have similarly high rates of reflux correction.

document_sections.heading: 3.3.2.3. Laparoscopic and robot-assisted laparoscopic techniques
document_sections.content: Case series support the feasibility of transperitoneal, extravesical, and pneumovesicoscopic intravesical reimplantation. A systematic review and meta-analysis comparing LEVUR and TVUR found both reasonable for resolution and complication outcomes. LEVUR is generally favoured in unilateral low-grade disease and currently appears to achieve higher success with a shorter hospital stay. Robotic antireflux procedures most commonly use an extravesical route. Of two recent systematic reviews examining OUR and RALUR, the first found RALUR feasible and effective for primary paediatric VUR, with success similar to OUR. The second found longer operations, greater costs, and more postoperative complications requiring another intervention with RALUR, but less postoperative pain and shorter admission than with OUR. Laparoscopic and robotic procedures are more invasive than endoscopic correction, while any advantage over open surgery remains under evaluation. Routine laparoscopic surgery therefore cannot currently be recommended; centres with established expertise may offer it to parents or caregivers as an alternative. Older children with complex anatomy or a failed injection or open reimplantation might benefit from the better exposure possible with RALUR. RALUR can be unilateral or bilateral, but bilateral surgery warrants caution because temporary urinary retention can occur. New hydronephrosis develops in up to 30% of cases after extravesical RALUR, at a rate similar to open ureteral reimplantation, and resolves without intervention in the overwhelming majority.

document_sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
document_sections.content: Genetic analyses have identified monogenic VUR causes and significant differences in innate-immunity and epithelial-function genes between children with VUR/febrile UTIs and controls. Diagnostic assessment should cover growth and general health, including height, weight, and blood pressure; febrile UTI; kidney status, including serum creatinine and GFR; reflux; and bladder and bowel function. Renal and bladder US is the standard first postnatal test. VCUG is recommended for bilateral high-grade hydronephrosis, duplex kidneys with lower-pole hydronephrosis and febrile breakthrough UTIs, a solitary kidney with hydronephrosis, ureteric dilatation, or abnormal bladders with a febrile UTI history, circumstances in which VUR is more likely. DMSA is the preferred agent for viewing renal cortex and differential kidney function. Screening asymptomatic siblings and offspring remains disputed. Febrile infection with abnormal renal US warrants VCUG because reflux risk is higher. Toilet-trained children with both LUTD and VUR face more recurrent febrile UTIs than those with reflux alone. BBD commonly accompanies febrile UTI in toilet-trained children regardless of primary VUR; combined BBD and VUR doubles recurrent febrile UTI risk. Children with UTI should therefore be evaluated carefully for BBD and treated for it before reflux management. Preserving kidney function is the main treatment aim. Nonsurgical options are observation, intermittent antibiotic prophylaxis or CAP, and bladder and bowel rehabilitation when LUTD is present. Conservative follow-up uses imaging and checks of height, weight, blood pressure, and possibly serum creatinine to assess reflux resolution and kidney status. Surgical options are endoscopic bulking-agent injection or open or minimally invasive ureteral reimplantation. CAP need not be given to every child with VUR; it generally uses daily antibiotics at a quarter to half of the usual therapeutic dose. In PREDICT, infants with grade III–V VUR and no previous UTI had a small but significant first-UTI prevention benefit with CAP, accompanied by more non-E. coli organisms and antibiotic resistance. Continuing CAP until BBD resolves is a practical approach. Initial medical management can be considered for febrile UTI with high-grade VUR; surgery is reserved for CAP nonadherence, febrile breakthrough UTI despite CAP, or persistently symptomatic reflux during prolonged follow-up. VUJO can appear late after endoscopic correction. High-grade reflux and dilated ureters increase late VUJO risk despite comparable success and obstruction rates during short-term (3–6 mo) follow-up. In infants with high-grade VUR, injection yields a higher resolution rate than CAP, but it cannot be recommended for every high-grade case because some children are asymptomatic. Potential spontaneous resolution or downgrading should be considered, particularly with unilateral reflux, lower grade, and efficient voiding. The ureteral diameter ratio is a new candidate predictor of outcomes and injection success. A systematic review and meta-analysis found LEVUR and TVUR suitable alternatives for resolution and complications. Extravesical access is the most common robotic antireflux approach; RALUR may be a feasible, effective option for primary paediatric VUR, with success equivalent to OUR.
